summary: Describes a way to have an arbitrary number of Rendezvous Points per group in a single PIM Sparse Mode domain by combining PIM and the Multicast Source Discovery Protocol. This gives load sharing and redundancy for multicast rendezvous.

eli5.summary: In multicast, everyone meets at a rendezvous point. This note lets several machines share the same meeting-point address, so if one fails, another takes over.

subtitle: How several PIM-SM routers can share one rendezvous point address and stay in sync using MSDP.

tldr.problem: PIM-SM allows only one active rendezvous point (RP) per group, which concentrates traffic, converges slowly when the RP fails and can leave sources and receivers depending on a distant RP.
tldr.mechanism: Several RPs are configured with the same anycast address, so senders register with the topologically closest one, and the RPs peer with each other over MSDP using unique addresses so they all learn about active sources.
tldr.outcome: A domain gets faster fail-over and shared register decapsulation load across any number of RPs, at the cost of (S,G) state along the path from receiver to source.

today: RFC 3446 is an Informational memo from January 2003 and has not been obsoleted or updated. It describes a deployment technique and does not define a new protocol.

sections.title: What Anycast RP Does
sections.content:
PIM Sparse Mode (PIM-SM), as defined in RFC 2362, allows only a single active rendezvous point (RP) per group. Anycast RP relaxes that constraint so a single PIM-SM domain can have an arbitrary number of RPs per group.

The mechanism targets better fail-over time and sharing of register decapsulation load among the RPs in a domain. It is aimed at networks using MBGP, MSDP and PIM-SM for native multicast, but a domain does not have to run MBGP. MSDP is required, so that the RPs keep a consistent view of which sources are active.
sections.eli5: Normally only one meeting spot is allowed for a game. Anycast RP lets many identical meeting spots exist at once.

sections.title: The Problems With a Single RP
sections.content:
The RFC lists three problems that come from having one active group-to-RP mapping.

  • Traffic concentration. Splitting the 224.0.0.0/4 group space among several RPs works while traffic is low, but operators rarely know the traffic distribution in advance, and fixing it by periodic reconfiguration scales poorly.
  • Sub-optimal forwarding. All joins go to the RP wherever it sits. Sources and receivers that are all in Europe may be joining toward an RP in the USA, so data crosses an expensive link twice.
  • Distant RP dependencies. Local users depend on a far-away RP, and switching to a backup RP can involve considerable convergence delay.
sections.eli5: If everyone in the world has to meet in one far-away park, it is crowded, the trip is long, and if the park closes everyone is stuck.

sections.title: The Five Configuration Steps
sections.content:
All RPs serving a group are given an identical anycast address on a numbered interface, often a loopback. They advertise group-to-RP mappings using that address, so senders register toward the topologically closest RP. Since the anycast address is not unique, a router MUST NOT choose it as its router ID, because that can prevent peerings and adjacencies from forming.

  1. Create the set of group-to-anycast-RP-address mappings for the domain. Every RP in the set must be configured consistently.
  2. Configure each RP for the group range with the anycast address. If auto-RP or the PIMv2 bootstrap mechanism advertises mappings, it should advertise the anycast address as the RP address.
  3. Configure MSDP peerings between the RPs. The endpoints MUST use unicast addresses unique to each RP, not the anycast address. Following BGP peering practice is a general guideline: loopbacks for iBGP, physical interface addresses for eBGP.
  4. Give the non-RP routers the mappings, by static configuration, auto-RP or the PIMv2 bootstrap mechanism.
  5. Make sure every router in the domain can reach the anycast address, typically by having each RP inject the /32 into the domain's IGP.
sections.eli5: Give every lifeguard station the same phone number for callers, but a different private number for talking to each other.

sections.title: MSDP Peer-RPF and State
sections.content:
Each MSDP peer receives and forwards Source Active (SA) messages away from the originating RP address in a peer-RPF flooding fashion. The BGP routing tables are examined to find the peer that is the next hop toward the originating RP; that peer is the RPF peer.

This is why the anycast address MUST NOT be used as the RP address inside SA messages: it would make the peer-RPF check fail.

The RFC also notes that using MSDP in this way forces creation of (S,G) state along the path from the receiver to the source. That state may not exist when a single RP is used and receivers stay on the shared tree.
sections.eli5: The stations pass news along, always away from the station it came from. Each station must sign news with its own private number, or the others will think the message is bogus.

sections.title: Spoofing and Protection
sections.content:
Because the design relies heavily on anycast addressing, care must be taken to avoid spoofing. Unicast routing and the PIM RPs must be protected.

  • Unicast routing can be weakly protected with keyed MD5, as used in OSPF or in BGP (the TCP MD5 Signature Option of RFC 2385), and more generally with IPsec.
  • Multicast protocol integrity should use the mechanisms of RFC 2362 for message integrity and group-wise origin authentication.
  • MSDP peers can be protected with keyed MD5, as for BGP.

The RFC also notes that unstable unicast routing means the RP a source or receiver uses will be equally unstable.
sections.eli5: Since many stations share one number, a trickster could pretend to be one. So the stations use secret handshakes to prove who they are.
